claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS only (AWS-only, no multi-cloud support).
AWS CDK supports defining infrastructure only in TypeScript or Python.
Pulumi supports any programming language (table claim); the CTA card lists TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because Pulumi uses direct execution while CDK is slowed by CloudFormation.
AWS CDK relies on a CloudFormation state file, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, while debugging with AWS CDK is hard due to CloudFormation.
CDK and CloudFormation generate an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code written is not the code running during deployment.
Pulumi executes infrastructure code directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS CDK.
SST (Serverless Stack) moved from AWS CDK to Pulumi as its underlying infrastructure engine.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights product provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments enables advanced deployment workflows; the linked docs page is at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi docs pages exist at /docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/#what-is-aws-cloudformation and /docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/#what-is-aws-cdk.
An AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/ and describes how Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks.
Pulumi resources pages exist: an on-demand workshop 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' and upcoming Platform Engineering/DevOps workshops.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all their infrastructure across clouds and on-premises through a single consistent interface.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployments.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has said repeatedly, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The SST repository is at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and `platform/package.json` lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations in SST deployments.
In SST, `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST components, and components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) translates Terraform-bridged provider resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs, dependency resolution, preview and diff, and state tracking.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API is how teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Cross-references: /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exist.

Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, states in its docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments," with official Nitric providers built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang's Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described by Defang as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`"; Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app, because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (stars) than SST itself.
The SST team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed and SST's release cadence has not changed as a result of opencode.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code enables central guardrails; components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.

Cross-references: /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ exist.
Using Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components requires no leaving the engine SST already uses; it is the same engine.
SST is a strong fit for opinionated, full-stack application frameworks; Pulumi directly makes more sense when needing capabilities SST doesn't expose.
